doc.title: George Masso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

title: Classroom teaching and developing listeners
summary: Masso would do more classroom teaching about active listening; they discuss the saturation of background music.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well we’ll talk about that a little down the road. So in your public education, after the war, it was band, ensemble, and did you do brass lessons?

Actually it was classroom teaching too, which I enjoyed very much. In fact I think if I had it to do over again, I would do almost exclusively classroom teaching and working with the lay people so to speak, those who are not involved in band, orchestra and so forth. Talk about music, and give them some background and reason for listening, and to try to develop active listening. Get them involved. I did have some very nice moments doing that, from junior high school right through high school, but I think if I had it to do over again I’d do it to a greater extent. Because I think there’s a need for that.
Boy, I do too, and we need future audiences.

To put it very bluntly, you know, to develop consumers that can go to concerts. I mean I’d encourage them to build libraries of CDs and whatever, and books, and go to concerts, with some background, and be able to evaluate what’s going on.
We seem to be somewhat saturated with media and music is everywhere, and I wonder sometimes if it makes it not quite as valuable.

I think you’re right and you know, it’s music to do something by. You get in the elevator they’ve got elevator music, supermarket music, they’ve got all kinds of background music. And people really aren’t listening.
